claim: An intuitive understanding of physical objects and events is critical for successfully interacting with the world.
source: An intuitive understanding of physical objects and events is critical for successfully interacting with the world.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of physical understanding, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Infants can differentiate liquids from solids by 5 months of age.
source: infants can differentiate liquids from solids by 5 months of age (Hespos et al., 2009; Hespos et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hespos et al., 2009 and 2016.

claim: Infants can infer an object's weight from its compression of a soft material by 11 months.
source: infer an object's weight from its compression of a soft material by 11 months (Hauf et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Hauf et al., 2012.

claim: Infants can use an object's center of mass to judge its stability on the edge of a surface by 12 months.
source: use an object's center of mass to judge its stability on the edge of a surface by 12 months (Baillargeon, 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Baillargeon, 1998.

claim: Human physical reasoning is fast and rich by adulthood.
source: By adulthood, human physical reasoning is fast and rich, and it generalizes across diverse real-world scenarios.
evidence: This is a general statement about adult physical reasoning based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Little is known about the brain basis of intuitive physics.
source: Yet little is known about the brain basis of intuitive physics, which could enable direct tests of computational models by revealing the relevant neural representations and their invariances and automaticity.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, based on inference from the literature.

claim: Model-free pattern recognition approaches to physical reasoning use deep neural networks.
source: A key distinction between computational models of intuitive physics is whether they use model-free pattern recognition (such as deep neural networks) (Lerer et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lerer et al., 2016.

claim: The generative approach models physical reasoning as approximate probabilistic inference over simulations in a physics engine.
source: The generative approach models physical reasoning as approximate probabilistic inference over simulations in a physics engine, an architecture with two core parts: an object-based representation of a 3D scene (which encodes many static variables, such as the size and mass of each object), and a model of physical forces that govern the scene's dynamics.
evidence: Supported by citation to Battaglia et al., 2013 in the preceding sentence.

claim: A physics engine has two core parts: an object-based representation of a 3D scene and a model of physical forces.
source: an architecture with two core parts: an object-based representation of a 3D scene (which encodes many static variables, such as the size and mass of each object), and a model of physical forces that govern the scene's dynamics.
evidence: This is a description of the physics engine architecture, drawing from established computational models.

claim: Simulation-based models can make robust inferences with accuracy comparable to human performance across many areas of physics.
source: Within this framework, simulation-based models can make robust inferences with accuracy comparable to human performance across many areas of physics, including collisions (Smith et al., 2013a), (Smith et al., 2013b), fluid dynamics (Bates et al., 2015), the motion of granular materials (Kubricht et al., 2016), and predictions about the outcome of applied forces (Ullman et al., 2018; Hamrick et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Smith et al., Bates et al., Kubricht et al., Ullman et al., and Hamrick et al.

claim: Specific regions in the parietal and frontal lobes are implicated in intuitive physical inference in humans.
source: A recent fMRI study has implicated specific regions in the parietal and frontal lobes in intuitive physical inference in humans (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2016.

claim: Candidate physics regions respond more strongly during a physical reasoning task than a difficulty-matched non-physical discrimination.
source: These regions responded more strongly during a physical reasoning task (which direction a tower of blocks will fall) than a difficulty-matched non-physical discrimination performed on the same stimuli
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2016 in the preceding sentence.

claim: Candidate physics regions respond more strongly during viewing of animated shapes depicting physical interactions than social interactions.
source: more strongly during viewing of animated shapes depicting physical interactions of inanimate objects than social interactions of agents (Fischer et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fischer et al., 2016.

claim: Candidate physics regions resemble regions previously implicated in action planning.
source: The candidate regions for intuitive physical inference found in this study resemble regions previously implicated in action planning (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Gallivan et al., 2014; Evarts and Thach, 1969; Loh et al., 2010; Chouinard et al., 2005; van Nuenen et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on action planning.

claim: Candidate physics regions resemble regions previously implicated in tool use.
source: and tool use (Gallivan et al., 2013; Brandi et al., 2014; Valyear et al., 2012; Goldenberg and Hagmann, 1998; Goldenberg and Spatt, 2009)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on tool use.

claim: Physical understanding is important for action planning and tool use.
source: consistent with the importance of physical understanding for these functions (Cant and Xu, 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Cant and Xu, 2012.

claim: It is unknown what candidate physics regions represent about physical events.
source: However, crucially, it is unknown what these regions represent about physical events.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Mass is the most basic scalar quantity that captures a property of all objects and governs motion in every physical interaction via Newton's second law.
source: Mass is not the only physical variable of interest, but it is the most basic scalar quantity that captures a property of all objects and that governs motion in every physical interaction, via Newton's second law.
evidence: This is based on established physics knowledge (Newton's second law).

claim: Participants were scanned with fMRI while performing physical inference, prediction, and orthogonal tasks on visually-presented stimuli.
source: Participants were scanned with fMRI while performing physical inference, prediction, and orthogonal tasks on visually-presented stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Each scanning session began with two runs of a localizer task to identify candidate regions engaged in physical reasoning.
source: Each scanning session began with two runs of a previously developed 'localizer' task (Figure 1a) to identify in each subject individually candidate regions engaged in physical reasoning (Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, with reference to Figure 1a and citation to Fischer et al., 2016.

claim: Pattern classification methods were applied to fMRI data to test for invariant representations of mass.
source: We then we applied pattern classification methods to fMRI data obtained from subjects viewing videos of dynamic objects, to test for invariant representations of mass in these regions (Fischer et al., 2016)
evidence: This describes the analytical approach used in the study.

claim: Six subjects participated in Experiment 1.
source: Six subjects were scanned using fMRI while viewing 3 s movies of real objects interacting in various physical scenarios
evidence: This is a description of the experimental sample.

claim: Experiment 1 used movies of objects splashing into water, being blown by a hairdryer, and falling onto a pillow.
source: Six subjects were scanned using fMRI while viewing 3 s movies of real objects interacting in various physical scenarios: splashing into a container of water, being blown across a flat surface by a hairdryer, and falling onto the soft surface of a pillow (Figure 1b).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in Experiment 1, with reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Three rigid 3D shapes of equal volume were used in Experiment 1.
source: Three rigid 3D shapes of equal volume were used (a rectangular prism, a cone, and a half-sphere)
evidence: This describes the stimuli design in Experiment 1.

claim: Movies in Experiment 1 were filmed for two different colors and two different masses of each shape.
source: and movies were filmed for two different colors and two different masses (45 g, 90 g) of each shape (36 total movies).
evidence: This describes the stimulus parameters in Experiment 1.

claim: Accuracy on the mass inference task in Experiment 1 was 88% across six subjects.
source: Accuracy on this task was 88% (i.e., percentage of responses matching the ground truth outcome) across six subjects.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data from Experiment 1.

claim: Situation-invariant mass decoding was significant in the candidate physics system with a group mean accuracy of 0.64.
source: This situation-invariant decoding was significant in the candidate physics system, with a group mean accuracy of 0.64 (p=0.0304, two-sided t-test, t-statistic = 2.9913, df = 5, significance threshold = 0.05).
evidence: This reports statistical results from the decoding analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: Mean classification accuracies across all three scenarios were greater than 50% in each subject in Experiment 1.
source: Mean classification accuracies across all three scenarios as well as classification accuracies for each left out scenario individually were greater than 50% in each subject.
evidence: This reports individual subject results from Experiment 1.

claim: Mass representations in Experiment 1 are not confounded with shape or color.
source: Further, mass representations are not confounded with shape or color, as colors and shapes were represented in equal proportions for both masses in the training and testing data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design controlling for shape and color.

claim: Decoding in Experiment 1 could not be based on the amount of motion in the videos.
source: Decoding could also not be based on the amount of motion in the videos, as heavy objects caused more motion in two of the conditions (splash, pillow), but did not move at all in the third (blow; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of motion across conditions.

claim: Decoding in Experiment 1 could not be based on specific motor responses.
source: Finally, decoding could not be based on specific motor responses, because the assignment of buttons to responses was switched halfway through the experiment, with equal an equal number of trials per button-press-to-response assignment represented in training and testing data.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design controlling for motor responses.

claim: Experiment 2 used a design that interleaves blocks of the mass task and a color task on the same stimuli.
source: To test this hypothesis, as well as the automaticity of the mass representation, we used a design that interleaves blocks of the mass task and a color task on the same stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Experiment 2.

claim: Six new subjects participated in Experiment 2.
source: In six new subjects, we replicated the findings of Experiment 1
evidence: This describes the sample for Experiment 2.

claim: Mean situation-invariant decoding accuracy in Experiment 2 during the mass task was 0.63.
source: mean situation-invariant decoding accuracy of 0.63 (across scenarios) was significantly above chance (p=0.0357, two-sided t-test, t-statistic = 2.853, df = 5)
evidence: This reports statistical results from Experiment 2 during the mass task.

claim: Decoding was found in 6 out of 6 subjects individually during the mass task in Experiment 2.
source: and decoding was found in 6 out of 6 subjects individually during the mass task (task accuracy 87%).
evidence: This reports individual subject results from Experiment 2.

claim: Task accuracy on the mass task in Experiment 2 was 87%.
source: and decoding was found in 6 out of 6 subjects individually during the mass task (task accuracy 87%).
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data from Experiment 2.

claim: Mass decoding was significantly above chance during the color task in Experiment 2.
source: More importantly, mass decoding was also significantly above chance (mean = 0.61, p=0.0033, two-sided t-test, t-statistic = 5.2576, df = 5), and present in each subject individually, during the color task.
evidence: This reports statistical results from Experiment 2 during the color task.

claim: Mass is represented even when the task does not require it.
source: This result shows that mass is represented even when the task does not require it
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the finding of mass decoding during the color task.

claim: The decoding of mass cannot be explained as an abstract response code.
source: and further that the decoding of mass we observe cannot be explained as an abstract response code.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of mass decoding during the color task where mass was not task-relevant.

claim: Color decoding from the same voxel activity during the color task was at chance in all subjects.
source: Further evidence against the idea that the mass representations reflect response codes comes from the fact that color decoding from the same voxel activity during the color task was at chance in all subjects.
evidence: This reports a null result for color decoding in Experiment 2.

claim: The candidate physics engine does not represent all task-relevant dimensions and may be more specific to physical variables.
source: Thus the candidate physics engine does not represent all task-relevant dimensions and may be more specific to physical variables.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that mass but not color could be decoded.

claim: Experiment 3 used 48 real-world movies of objects sliding down a ramp and colliding with a puck.
source: We created 48 real-world movies. Each 6 s video shows an object (made of aluminum, cardboard, lego, or cork) sliding down a ramp and colliding with a puck (half-ping-pong ball), whose initial location is consistent between videos (Figure 2b).
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in Experiment 3, with reference to Figure 2b.

claim: In Experiment 3, subjects answered whether they predict the sliding object will launch the puck across a black line.
source: In the task, subjects answer (as immediately as possible) whether they predict the sliding object will launch the puck across a black line, which can lie in three different locations.
evidence: This describes the task in Experiment 3.

claim: The stimuli in Experiment 3 were designed to orthogonalize mass, friction, and motion.
source: Importantly, these stimuli were designed in a way that orthogonalizes mass, friction, and motion in the videos (Figure 2a)
evidence: This describes the stimulus design in Experiment 3, with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Accuracy in the prediction task in Experiment 3 was 71% across 20 subjects.
source: Accuracy in the prediction task was 71% across 20 subjects.
evidence: This reports behavioral performance data from Experiment 3.

claim: Mass can be decoded from candidate physics regions in Experiment 3 with mean accuracy of 0.60.
source: Experiment 3 replicated once again our finding that mass can be decoded from candidate physics regions (mean accuracy of 0.60 was significant, p=0.0392, two-sided t-test, t-statistic = 2.2152, df = 19, significance threshold = 0.05 ).
evidence: This reports statistical results from the decoding analysis in Experiment 3.

claim: Mass decoding in Experiment 3 required generalization across friction and material of the object.
source: Further, this experiment demonstrates an important new invariance of these mass representations beyond those already found in Experiments 1 and 2: the mass decoding in Experiment 3 required generalization across the friction and material of the object shown (lego to cork for heavy, and cardboard to aluminum for light)
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design where training and testing used different materials and friction levels.

claim: Mass decoding in Experiment 3 required generalization across the amount of motion in the videos.
source: as well as generalization across the amount of motion in the videos (calculated by measuring the amount of optical flow; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and optical flow measurements.

claim: Eye movements were recorded for 6 subjects in Experiment 3 to verify fixation and ensure mass decoding was independent of eye movement.
source: Eye movements were recorded for 6 subjects, to verify that subjects were fixating and to ensure that mass decoding was independent of eye movement (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes an additional control measure in Experiment 3.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed no significant effects of mass or friction on mean eye position or mean saccade amplitude.
source: A two-way ANOVA with mass and friction as repeated-measures factors revealed no significant effects at the .05 significance level of mass or friction on mean eye position (mass: F1,3 = 0.084, p=0.79; friction: F1,3 = 0.31, p=0.62) or mean saccade amplitude (mass: F1,3 = 0.28, p=0.63; friction: F1,3 = 0.46, p=0.55)
evidence: This reports statistical results from eye movement analysis in Experiment 3.

claim: It is unlikely that eye movements could explain the decoding results in Experiment 3.
source: so it is unlikely that eye movements could explain our decoding results.
evidence: This is an inference based on the null results from eye movement analysis.

claim: A localizer task based on the contrast of object textures and ensembles versus their scrambled counterparts was used to identify LO and texture-sensitive regions of OTC.
source: Following Gallivan et al., we used a localizer task (Cant and Xu, 2012) based on the contrast of object textures and ensembles versus their scrambled counterparts, to identify LO and texture-sensitive regions of OTC in six participants completing the ramp task in the same session.
evidence: This describes an additional localizer task used in Experiment 3, with citation to Cant and Xu, 2012.

claim: Invariant mass decoding did not reach significance in LO during Experiment 3.
source: Although these subjects showed reliable decoding of a mass representation invariant to friction, material, and motion in candidate physics regions during the physical prediction task (Experiment 3), this invariant decoding did not reach significance in LO (p=0.39)
evidence: This reports a null result for mass decoding in LO.

claim: Invariant mass decoding did not reach significance in OTC during Experiment 3.
source: or in OTC (p=0.67) during the same task.
evidence: This reports a null result for mass decoding in OTC.

claim: Parietal and frontal regions previously implicated in intuitive physics compute an abstract representation of mass useful in a generalized model of physics.
source: While the parietal and frontal regions previously implicated in intuitive physics are recruited to compute an abstract representation of mass useful in a generalized model of physics
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of invariant mass decoding in these regions.

claim: Regions in the ventral stream may be recruited to infer object mass tied to scene- and task-specific cues.
source: regions in the ventral stream, canonically associated with visual pattern recognition, may be recruited to infer object mass tied to scene- and task-specific cues such as the visual appearance of object material.
evidence: This is speculation based on the null results in ventral stream regions and their known functions.

claim: A whole-brain random-effects group analysis was performed for the physics >color contrast using all data from the toppling towers localizer.
source: We used all data (two runs per subject) from the toppling towers localizer to perform a whole-brain random-effects group analysis for the physics >color contrast (Figure 3A).
evidence: This describes the group-level analysis performed, with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: The group analysis identifies a map of brain regions, primarily premotor and parietal areas, preferentially engaged in physical reasoning.
source: This group analysis identifies a map of brain regions, primarily premotor and parietal areas, that was first shown in Fischer et al. (2016) to be preferentially engaged in physical reasoning, and is now replicated here in 32 new subjects.
evidence: This reports the results of the group analysis, with citation to Fischer et al., 2016.

claim: The candidate physics network encodes an abstract, generalizable representation of object mass that can be decoded from individual subject fROIs in 31 out of 32 subjects.
source: We further demonstrate that this candidate physics network encodes an abstract, generalizable representation of object mass that can be decoded from individual subject fROIs (see Materials and methods) in 31 out of 32 subjects (Figure 3B).
evidence: This reports the main finding across all subjects, with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: In a network of parietal and frontal brain regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference, robust decoding of object mass was found, replicated across three experiments and present numerically in 31 out of 32 participants.
source: In a network of parietal and frontal brain regions previously implicated in intuitive physical inference, and replicated here in a larger sample (see Figure 3), we find robust decoding of object mass, replicated across three experiments and present numerically in 31 out of 32 participants.
evidence: This summarizes the main finding of the study, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The mass representation is invariant to the scenario revealing the object's mass, as well as to object material, friction, and motion energy.
source: Critically, this mass representation is invariant to the scenario revealing the object's mass (splashing, falling, and blowing), as well as to object material, friction, and motion energy.
evidence: This summarizes the key invariances demonstrated across the three experiments.

claim: The study presents the first neural evidence of a mass representation underlying physical reasoning with invariance that supports flexible, generalizable navigation of the physical world.
source: Here we present the first neural evidence of a mass representation underlying physical reasoning with invariance that supports this kind of flexible, generalizable navigation of the physical world.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: Among current computational models, structured generative models such as physics engines best exhibit the capacity for generalization found in human physical reasoning.
source: Among current computational models, those that best exhibit this capacity for generalization are structured generative models such as physics engines (Battaglia et al., 2013; Yildirim et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Battaglia et al., 2013 and Yildirim et al., 2019.

claim: The network of frontal and parietal fROIs implements in some form a causal generative model of physical objects and their dynamics.
source: supporting the hypothesis that the network of frontal and parietal fROIs we identify implements in some form a causal generative model of physical objects and their dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the invariant mass representations found and comparison to computational models.

claim: Neural representations underlying physical reasoning have only been studied in action planning tasks to date.
source: To date, neural representations underlying physical reasoning have only been studied in action planning tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Gallivan et al. (2014) used multivariate decoding methods to find representations of object mass in ventral visual pathway areas during action planning.
source: Gallivan et al. (2014). used multivariate decoding methods to find, in multivoxel activity patterns during action planning, representations of object mass in ventral visual pathway areas, specifically the lateral occipital complex (LO), posterior fusiform sulcus (pFs), and texture-sensitive regions of occipitotemporal cortex (OTC), in addition to motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallivan et al., 2014.

claim: Mass information for action planning is known to be represented in motor cortex (M1) and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd).
source: where mass information for action planning is known to be represented (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Evarts and Thach, 1969; Loh et al., 2010; Chouinard et al., 2005; van Nuenen et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies on motor planning.

claim: Prior studies have provided evidence for representations of mass only when participants are performing action planning tasks.
source: First, prior studies have provided evidence for representations of mass (Johansson and Flanagan, 2009; Gallivan et al., 2014; Evarts and Thach, 1969; Loh et al., 2010; Chouinard et al., 2005; van Nuenen et al., 2012) only when participants are performing action planning tasks.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The current study shows that mass representations are available when subjects are not asked about mass per se.
source: In contrast, we show that these representations are available when subjects are not asked about mass per se, for instance in the ramp task where mass is relevant to the task but not explicitly reported, and in the color task where mass is not relevant at all.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: Prior studies have decoded representations of mass only within a particular stimulus or scenario.
source: Second, and more importantly, prior studies have decoded representations of mass only within a particular stimulus or scenario, whereas our study finds abstract representations of mass that generalize across scenarios and are invariant to friction, material, and motion.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work and the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The abstractness and invariance of the mass representations suggest they reflect inputs to a physics engine in the brain rather than just another dimension of visual pattern classification.
source: It is the abstractness and invariance of the mass representations reported here that suggests they reflect not just another dimension of visual pattern classification, but the generalizability expected of inputs to a physics engine in the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the mass representations found.

claim: Invariant representations of mass are found in a network of frontal and parietal regions that support machinery for a neural physics engine.
source: These invariant representations of mass are found in a network of frontal and parietal regions (Figure 3) that we suggest support machinery for a neural physics engine.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Similar frontal and parietal regions have been implicated in thinking about physical concepts presented as words.
source: Similar frontal and parietal regions have been implicated in thinking about physical concepts presented as words (Mason and Just, 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mason and Just, 2016.

claim: The physics network represents abstract, generalizable physical concepts rather than low-level visual features or situation-specific representations.
source: supporting the hypothesis that this network represents abstract, generalizable physical concepts rather than low-level visual features or situation-specific representations of physical variables.
evidence: This is an inference based on the invariant representations found and comparison to other studies.

claim: Invariant mass representations were not found in ventral visual pathway areas such as LOC and OTC in tasks not requiring action planning.
source: We did not find invariant mass representations in ventral visual pathway areas such as LOC and OTC (in tasks not requiring action planning)
evidence: This reports a null result for ventral stream regions.

claim: LOC may not play a causal role in computing object weight.
source: suggesting that LOC may not play a causal role in computing object weight. This supports previous findings by Buckingham et al. (2018), which showed that a patient with bilateral lesions including LOC had a preserved ability to judge object weight (Buckingham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Buckingham et al., 2018.

claim: When ventral visual areas represent motor-relevant object properties, it may be a top-down effect driven by the motor planning process where representations are tied to specific tasks.
source: This overarching pattern of results suggests that when ventral visual areas do represent motor-relevant object properties (Gallivan et al., 2014), it may be a top-down effect driven by the motor planning process where representations are tied to specific tasks.
evidence: This is speculation based on the pattern of results and comparison to Gallivan et al., 2014.

claim: It remains unknown how the brain estimates generalizable physical properties of objects from visual inputs.
source: It remains unknown how the brain estimates generalizable physical properties of objects from visual inputs.
evidence: This is a statement about an open question in the field.

claim: Feed-forward inference methods akin to deep-learning based recognition models may be integrated with generative models to provide efficient inference of physical properties.
source: It could be that feed-forward inference methods, akin to deep-learning based recognition models, are integrated with generative models and provide an efficient means of inference of physical properties that then serve as inputs to physics engines. This account has been explored computationally and has received behavioral support (Yildirim et al., 2019)
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to Yildirim et al., 2019.

claim: At the level of prediction and inference, intuitive physics recruits brain regions and representations outside the ventral stream.
source: Our results show that at the level of prediction and inference, intuitive physics recruits brain regions and representations outside the ventral stream, the canonical locus of visual pattern recognition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Six subjects participated in Experiment 1 (ages 21–26; 3 male, 3 female).
source: Six subjects (ages 21–26; 3 male, 3 female) participated in Experiment 1
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 1.

claim: Six subjects participated in Experiment 2 (ages 21–40; 3 male, 3 female).
source: six (ages 21–40; 3 male, 3 female) in Experiment 2
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 2.

claim: Twenty subjects participated in Experiment 3 (ages 20–32; 9 male, 11 female).
source: and twenty (ages 20–32; 9 male, 11 female) in Experiment 3.
evidence: This describes the participant demographics for Experiment 3.

claim: All participants were right-handed and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
source: All participants were right-handed and had normal or corrected to normal vision.
evidence: This describes inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board approved all experimental protocols.
source: The Massachusetts Institute of Technology Institutional Review Board approved all experimental protocols.
evidence: This describes ethical approval for the study.

claim: The localizer task used movies depicting stacks of blocks created in Blender 2.70.
source: In each experiment, participants performed 2 runs of a 7 min 'localizer' fMRI task from Fischer et al. (2016), in which subjects viewed 6 s movies depicting stacks ('towers') of yellow, blue, and white blocks created in Blender 2.70 (Blender Foundation).
evidence: This describes the stimuli creation method for the localizer task.

claim: The block towers in the localizer were constructed to be unstable such that they would topple if gravity were to take effect.
source: The block towers were constructed to be unstable such that they would topple if gravity were to take effect.
evidence: This describes the design of the localizer stimuli.

claim: Each scanning run for the localizer task consisted of 23 18 s blocks: 10 blocks of the physical task, 10 blocks of the color task, and 3 rest blocks.
source: Each scanning run for this localizer task (2 per subject) consisted of 23 18 s blocks: 10 blocks of the physical task, 10 blocks of the color task, and 3 rest blocks, which consisted of a black screen with a fixation cross.
evidence: This describes the structure of the localizer task runs.

claim: Objects in Experiment 1 were constructed from Learning Resources 'View-Thru Geometric Solids.'
source: Objects were constructed by hand from Learning Resources 'View-Thru Geometric Solids.'
evidence: This describes the materials used to create stimuli in Experiment 1.

claim: The 'light' objects in Experiment 1 were left empty (45 g), and the 'heavy' objects were filled with a mixture of lead pellets and flour (90 g).
source: Two different masses were created for each object: the 'light' objects were left empty (45 g), and the 'heavy' objects were filled with a mixture of lead pellets and flour (90 g), and painted the same color.
evidence: This describes how different masses were created for Experiment 1 stimuli.

claim: The visual appearance of the objects in Experiment 1 was identical across masses.
source: The visual appearance of the objects was identical across masses, only the object's physical behavior could be used to infer its mass.
evidence: This describes a key control in the stimulus design of Experiment 1.

claim: The mass and color tasks in Experiment 2 were matched for difficulty using data collected from 50 workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
source: The two judgment types were matched for difficulty using data collected from 50 workers with normal color vision on Amazon Mechanical Turk.
evidence: This describes a control procedure for Experiment 2.

claim: Mean accuracy on the mass task in the Mechanical Turk pilot was 86.2% (±2.4 SD).
source: Mean accuracy on the mass task was 86.2% (±2.4 SD)
evidence: This reports behavioral data from the pilot study for Experiment 2.

claim: Mean accuracy on the color task in the Mechanical Turk pilot was 89% (±3.6 SD).
source: mean accuracy on the color task was 89% (±3.6 SD).
evidence: This reports behavioral data from the pilot study for Experiment 2.

claim: Materials in Experiment 3 were selected to orthogonalize mass and friction.
source: Object materials were selected to orthogonalize mass and friction, object material, and motion.
evidence: This describes the stimulus design rationale for Experiment 3.

claim: Coefficients of friction in Experiment 3 were found by taking the tangent of the angle of incline at which the object starts to slide down the ramp at constant speed.
source: Coefficients of friction were found by taking of the tangent of the angle of incline at which the object starts to slide down the ramp at constant speed, after being tapped.
evidence: This describes the method for measuring friction in Experiment 3.

claim: Motion in the videos of Experiment 3 was calculated using the Optical Flow package in Matlab 2016.
source: Motion in the videos was calculated using the Optical Flow package in Matlab 2016.
evidence: This describes the method for quantifying motion in Experiment 3.

claim: The most motion in Experiment 3 videos was found in the movies with lego blocks.
source: The most motion was found in the movies with lego blocks (x = 1.1848 e+04, y = 1.8065e+04), followed by aluminum (x = 1.0781e+04, y = 1.767e+04), cardboard (x = 9.6789e+03, y = 1.4150e+04), and cork (x = 9.0324e+03, y = 1.4126e+04).
evidence: This reports optical flow measurements for different materials in Experiment 3.

claim: Imaging was performed on a Siemens 3T MAGNETOM Tim Trio Scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
source: Imaging was performed at the Athinoula A. Martinos Imaging Center at MIT on a Siemens 3T MAGNETOM Tim Trio Scanner with a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI equipment used.

claim: Eye tracking data were preprocessed with EyeLink Data Viewer software and analyzed in MATLAB R2016B.
source: Eye tracking data were preprocessed with EyeLink Data Viewer software and analyzed in MATLAB R2016B (The MathWorks).
evidence: This describes the analysis pipeline for eye tracking data.

claim: Data preprocessing and general linear models were performed using FsFast tools in the FreeSurfer Software Suite.
